catholic.salvation:
Catholics speak of salvation as God's work of delivering the human race from sin and death and bringing people into friendship with him through Jesus Christ. It begins in this life by grace, ordinarily through Baptism, and is meant to reach its fullness in the vision of God. Justification is part of this same gift: God not only forgives sin but makes the sinner righteous by the grace of Christ living in the soul.

Salvation is not treated as a single past moment that cannot be lost. A person may fall from grace by mortal sin and be restored through repentance and the sacrament of Reconciliation. Good works done in grace are fruits of that life, not a private claim on God. The Church prays for the salvation of all while teaching that Christ is the one Savior and that the Church is the ordinary way he has given.
catholic.communion:
Catholics call this sacrament the Eucharist, and the liturgy in which it is celebrated the Mass. In it the bread and wine become the Body and Blood of Christ. The Mass is both a sacred meal of communion with the risen Lord and the making present of his once-for-all sacrifice of the Cross.

Receiving Communion means receiving Christ himself, not a mere sign of him. The Church asks that those who receive be baptized, be in communion with the Catholic Church, and be in a state of grace. The Eucharist is the source and summit of Catholic life: other sacraments and the whole of prayer point toward it and flow from it.
catholic.trinity:
The Trinity is the central mystery of Catholic faith: one God in three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, coequal and coeternal, not three gods and not three passing masks of one person. The persons are distinct in their relations of origin: the Father is unbegotten, the Son is begotten of the Father, the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. They are one in essence, one in will, one in action toward the world.

Catholics confess this faith in the Nicene Creed and in Baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The mystery is not a puzzle to be solved but the living God who has made himself known. All prayer, all sacraments, and the whole of salvation history are read as the work of this one God who is a communion of persons.
catholic.father:
God the Father is the First Person of the Trinity, the unbegotten source of the Son and, with the Son, of the Holy Spirit. Catholics address him as Father because Christ taught his disciples to do so and because, by grace, the baptized are adopted as sons and daughters in the Son.

The Father is not a remote first cause. He sends the Son and the Spirit, receives the offering of the Mass, and is the end of all created desire. Catholic prayer is offered to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. When Catholics speak of God without further qualification they often mean the one divine nature shared by the three persons, but 'God the Father' names the person from whom the other two proceed.
catholic.holy_spirit:
The Holy Spirit is the Third Person of the Trinity, consubstantial with the Father and the Son, adored and glorified with them. Catholics confess that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is poured out on the Church. He is the Paraclete, the Advocate promised by Christ, who dwells in the baptized, gives life to the sacraments, and distributes charisms for the building up of the Church.

Confirmation is understood as a special strengthening by this same Spirit. Scripture is read as inspired by him. The Church does not treat the Spirit as an impersonal force or as a later title for the Father. Personal prayer, the liturgy, and the moral life are all the Spirit's work in those who do not resist him.
catholic.filioque:
In the Latin Creed Catholics say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, the Filioque. The Church understands this as a statement about the inner life of God: the Spirit is not a second Son, but proceeds from the Father as from the one source and also from the Son, because Father and Son are one in the gift of the Spirit.

This wording was added in the West and remains part of the ordinary Catholic profession of faith. Catholic teaching also holds that the Father remains the first origin of the Spirit. The phrase is not meant to divide the Trinity or to deny what the Eastern churches confess about the Father as source. It names, in Latin theological language, the one procession of the one Spirit.
catholic.essence_and_energies:
Catholics speak first of the one divine essence, the Godhead shared wholly by Father, Son, and Spirit. God is simple: not composed of parts. What God does in the world does not split that essence. Grace in the soul is commonly described as created grace, a real share in God's life given to the creature, distinct from God's own uncreated being, together with the indwelling of the divine persons themselves.

Catholic theology has used other languages as well, including talk of God's operations and of uncreated gifts. The essential claim is that God truly communicates himself without the creature becoming a fourth person of the Trinity. The distinction some Eastern writers draw between essence and energies is not the ordinary Catholic vocabulary, though Catholics can recognize in it a concern they share: God is beyond comprehension and yet truly present and active in those he sanctifies.
catholic.incarnation:
The Incarnation is the mystery that the eternal Son, the Word, took flesh and became man in the womb of the Virgin Mary. He is one person, the divine Son, who now has two natures, divine and human, without confusion or separation. Catholics confess this in the Creed: he was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, and became man.

The Incarnation is not a costume or a later adoption of a merely human Jesus. From the first moment of his human life he is true God and true man. All of Catholic sacramental life rests on this: God has joined himself to our nature so that our nature may be joined to God. Christmas, the Angelus, and the title Mother of God all hang on this confession.
catholic.natures_of_christ:
Catholics hold the Chalcedonian teaching of two natures in the one person of Christ: he is fully God and fully man, consubstantial with the Father in divinity and consubstantial with us in humanity, except for sin. The union is hypostatic, that is, in the person of the Word. The natures are not mixed into a third thing, nor are they two persons acting side by side.

From this follow the Church's titles and prayers. Mary is Mother of God because the one she bore is the Son. The human acts of Jesus, including his suffering and death, are the acts of the divine person in his human nature, and so they save. Catholic preaching resists both a Christ who is only divine in appearance and a Christ who is a holy man later linked to God.
catholic.virgin_birth:
Catholics confess the virgin birth and, more precisely, the virginal conception of Jesus: he was conceived in Mary's womb by the Holy Spirit without a human father. The Creed states that he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. This is taught as a real event in history, not only as a symbol of spiritual newness.

The virgin birth belongs with the Church's faith in who Jesus is. It does not mean that his humanity is incomplete. He is born of a woman and is truly man. Mary's yes, the Annunciation, and the feast of Christmas keep this teaching in the Church's prayer. Related but distinct is the further Catholic conviction of her perpetual virginity.
catholic.preexistence_of_christ:
Catholics confess the Son as the eternal Son, begotten of the Father before all ages. He did not begin to exist when he was conceived in Mary. The Word was with God and was God, and that same Word became flesh. Eternal generation names the Son's relation to the Father in the Trinity; the Incarnation names his taking of a human nature in time.

This rules out treating Jesus as a creature, however exalted, who was later raised to divine rank. The Church's worship of Christ, the Gloria, and the preface of the Trinity all assume that the one who walked in Galilee is the one through whom all things were made. Preexistence here means eternity as God, not a previous created life.
catholic.atonement:
Catholics speak of the atonement as Christ's redemptive work: by his obedient life, death, and resurrection he reconciles the world to the Father. The Cross is a true sacrifice, the fulfillment of Israel's offerings and the act in which the Son offers himself in love. Satisfaction language is used to say that he makes good what sin has broken, not that the Father is a third party demanding payment from an innocent bystander.

The fruits of this work are given through faith and the sacraments. No later Mass adds a new Calvary; the one sacrifice is made present. Catholic preaching holds together several biblical images: victory over death, ransom, sacrificial offering, and the healing of human nature. All of them name the same deed of the incarnate Son.
catholic.resurrection_of_christ:
The Resurrection is the Father's vindication of the crucified Son and the beginning of the new creation. Catholics confess that Jesus truly died, was buried, and on the third day rose bodily. The risen Lord is the same Jesus, with a glorified body, not a ghost and not a mere symbol of hope.

Easter is the feast around which the liturgical year turns. Sunday worship, Baptism as dying and rising with Christ, and the hope of the resurrection of the body all rest on this event. The Church treats the empty tomb and the appearances as part of the apostolic witness, not as optional decoration on a spiritual lesson.
catholic.ascension:
The Ascension is Christ's going to the Father with his glorified humanity and his sitting at the right hand of the Father. It is not an escape from the world but the exaltation of our nature in him and the opening of heaven to those who belong to him. From there he sends the Spirit and remains present in the Church, especially in the Eucharist.

Catholics keep the Ascension as a holy day in the calendar. It grounds prayer in Christ's name: the priestly intercession of Jesus continues. It also frames Christian hope. The one who ascended will return, and the humanity he took with him is the pledge of what the redeemed are meant to become.
catholic.gifts_of_the_spirit:
Catholics speak of the gifts of the Holy Spirit both as the seven gifts named in the tradition of Isaiah and Confirmation, such as wisdom and fortitude, and as charisms given for the service of the Church. These charisms, whether quiet or striking, are ordered to holiness and to the common good, and they are discerned within the Church rather than used as private proof of standing.

The Spirit's ordinary gifts include the theological virtues and the grace of the sacraments. Extraordinary gifts have appeared in every age and are neither demanded of every Catholic nor dismissed as impossible. The measure is charity and communion with the Church.
catholic.baptism_in_the_spirit:
Some Catholics, especially in the charismatic renewal, speak of baptism in the Spirit as a fresh yielding to the Holy Spirit already given in Baptism and Confirmation. The Church does not treat this as an eighth sacrament or as the first real reception of the Spirit. It is a pastoral way of describing a deeper release of what was already conferred.

Official teaching remains that the Spirit is given in the sacraments of initiation. Charismatic prayer groups exist with the Church's recognition in many places, and they are asked to stay within Catholic doctrine and under the bishop. Other Catholics never use the phrase and live the same sacramental life without it.
catholic.tongues:
The gift of tongues is known in Catholic history from the New Testament onward and is present in some Catholic charismatic communities today. The Church treats it as a possible charism, to be tested by its fruit and by order in worship, not as the required sign that a person has received the Spirit.

Most Catholic liturgy does not include tongues. When the gift is exercised, it is meant to build up prayer and is subject to pastoral guidance. Catholics do not hold that every Christian must speak in tongues, nor that the gift vanished forever after the apostles. They also do not treat unintelligible speech as a substitute for the Church's public worship in a known tongue.
catholic.continuationism:
Catholics hold that charisms continue in the Church. The Spirit who worked in the apostles still gives gifts as he wills. Miracles, healings, and prophecy are not declared finished, though public revelation that binds the whole Church is held to have ended with the apostles.

Discernment belongs to the Church. Private revelations and alleged miracles may be approved, tolerated, or rejected. Catholic life does not depend on constant signs; it depends on Word, sacrament, and charity. The possibility of gifts today is simply part of believing that the Spirit has not abandoned the Church.
catholic.justification:
Justification is the gracious act by which God, through Christ, turns a sinner from the state of sin to the state of grace and of adoption. Catholics teach that it is not only a legal declaration. God forgives and also makes the person righteous by infusing grace and charity into the soul. Initial justification is a gift, unearned, ordinarily given in Baptism.

Once justified, a person cooperates with grace. Justification can increase through good works done in Christ, and it can be lost by mortal sin and restored in Reconciliation. Faith is the beginning of this life, but a living faith works through love. The Council of Trent remains the classic Catholic statement of this teaching.
catholic.sanctification:
Sanctification is growth in holiness, the unfolding of the life given in justification. Catholics do not draw a hard wall between being declared just and being made holy. The same grace that justifies begins to heal and raise the person. The sacraments, prayer, fasting, works of mercy, and fidelity in vocation are ordinary paths of this growth.

Perfection is not claimed as a finished earthly state for most people. The saints show that real transformation is possible. Sanctification is God's work first, and it asks a free response. It aims at charity, the love of God and neighbor, not at a private spiritual polish.
catholic.glorification:
Glorification is the completion of salvation in the resurrection of the body and the beatific vision, the seeing of God face to face. Those who die in God's grace and are purified, if need be, enter this life. It is gift, not wages, yet it crowns a life lived in Christ.

Catholic hope is bodily as well as spiritual. Heaven is not the discarding of human nature but its fulfillment. The liturgy of All Saints and the prayers for the dead keep this end in view. Marys Assumption is confessed as an anticipated share in this same glorification.
catholic.theosis:
Catholics speak of divinization or of becoming partakers of the divine nature. By grace the baptized share in God's own life without ceasing to be creatures. The goal is union with the Trinity, not absorption into an impersonal divine substance and not becoming a fourth divine person.

This language is at home in the Fathers and in the liturgy even when everyday Catholic speech prefers 'holiness' or 'sanctifying grace.' The Eucharist, in which the faithful receive Christ, is a chief means of this sharing. Eastern Catholic churches often use the word theosis more readily; the Latin tradition teaches the same destiny under other words.
catholic.grace:
Grace is God's free gift of his own life. Catholics distinguish sanctifying grace, the habitual gift that makes the soul holy and pleasing to God, from actual graces, the particular helps by which God prompts and sustains good acts. Grace is not a created thing standing in for God; it is God's self-gift, spoken of also as a created effect in us so that the creature is truly changed.

Grace does not destroy freedom. It heals and raises it. The sacraments confer grace because Christ acts in them. No one earns the first grace. Cooperation after that first gift is itself grace at work. Catholic moral teaching assumes that without grace the call of the Gospel cannot be lived.
catholic.faith_and_works:
Catholics confess that a person is justified by grace through faith, and that this faith is living when it works through love. Works done apart from grace do not purchase salvation. Works done in grace are the fruit and growth of justification, not a rival system beside Christ.

The letter of James is read with Paul, not against him. Faith without works is dead. At the same time the Church rejects any picture in which a sinner presents a stack of merits as a claim God must honor. Merit, in Catholic speech, is God's crowning of his own gifts. The saints are examples of this cooperation, not exceptions to grace.
catholic.predestination:
Catholics teach predestination as God's eternal plan to bring the redeemed to glory. God desires the salvation of all and does not predestine anyone to evil. Those who are saved are saved by his gracious initiative; those who are lost are lost by their own free refusal.

Within that frame Catholic theologians have differed on how grace and freedom meet, from more Augustinian accounts to views that stress the real possibility of refusal. The Church has not defined one school as the only Catholic one. What it will not say is that God is the author of sin or that human freedom is a fiction. Prayer for perseverance assumes both God's sovereignty and a freedom that can still say no.
catholic.election:
Election names God's choosing of a people and of persons for a purpose of grace. Israel is elect; the Church is elect; individuals are called. Catholics do not treat election as a hidden list that makes the sacraments play-acting. The call is issued in history through the Gospel and Baptism.

Election is for holiness and for mission, not for private privilege. The Church warns against trying to read the eternal decrees by guessing who is in and who is out. One lives the call by remaining in Christ. Corporate election of the Church and personal vocation sit together in Catholic speech.
catholic.perseverance:
Final perseverance is itself a gift. Catholics pray for it and do not claim they can secure it by a past decision alone. A justified person can lose sanctifying grace by mortal sin. Restoration is possible through repentance and Reconciliation.

This is why Catholic life includes examination of conscience, frequent confession for many, and prayer against presumption and against despair. The Church also rejects anxious fear that God is unwilling to save. Perseverance is hoped for because God is faithful, and it is worked out because freedom remains real until death.
catholic.assurance:
Catholics are taught to have a firm hope of salvation, grounded in God's promises, the sacraments, and a life of charity, without claiming an absolute, unassailable certainty about their own final perseverance apart from a special revelation. One may be sure that God is faithful and that the sacraments do what they signify. One may not treat one's own future freedom as already finished.

Pastoral practice encourages peace, not scrupulosity. The point of refusing a certain kind of assurance is not to keep people nervous. It is to keep hope honest: we are saved in hope, and we watch and pray.
catholic.repentance:
Repentance is conversion of heart, sorrow for sin because it offends God, and the resolve to change. Catholics call the interior act contrition. Perfect contrition arises from love of God; imperfect contrition arises from fear of punishment or from the ugliness of sin. Both are used by God; the sacrament of Reconciliation is the ordinary way grave sin is forgiven after Baptism.

Repentance is not a single emotional crisis. It is a habit of returning. Lent, Friday penance, and the confession of venial sins train this habit. Without repentance, ritual is empty. With it, even a long absence from the Church can be healed.
catholic.means_of_grace:
Catholics speak of the sacraments as the principal means of grace Christ left in the Church. They are not human ceremonies laid on top of an already finished gift. In them Christ himself acts. The Word of God, prayer, and works of mercy also convey grace, but the seven sacraments have a special place as signs that effect what they signify.

Baptism, Confirmation, and the Eucharist initiate and feed the life of grace. Reconciliation and Anointing of the Sick heal it. Holy Orders and Matrimony order it toward mission and family. Catholics do not treat grace as automatic magic. The sacrament gives what it promises when received with the right disposition, and God is not bound by the sacraments in such a way that he cannot act outside them.
catholic.original_sin:
Original sin is the wound inherited from the first human disobedience. Catholics teach that Adam's sin lost original holiness for the race. Each person is conceived without that first grace, inclined to sin, and in need of salvation, even before personal faults. Baptism remits original sin and gives sanctifying grace, though the inclination called concupiscence remains to be struggled with.

Original sin is not a personal crime of the infant. It is a privation and a state. Catholic teaching rejects both the idea that human nature is untouched by the Fall and the idea that infants are personally guilty in the way an adult sinner is. The Immaculate Conception of Mary is confessed as a unique preservation from this wound, by the merits of Christ.
catholic.human_nature:
Catholics describe human nature as created good, in the image of God, and wounded by sin rather than destroyed. Reason and freedom remain real. They are not enough, without grace, to reach the supernatural end for which God made us. Concupiscence pulls the will, but it is not itself original sin after Baptism.

This wounded nature is assumed by the Son in the Incarnation and healed in the sacraments. Catholic moral teaching therefore speaks to people as responsible agents who need grace, not as wrecks incapable of any truth or as innocents who need only education. Body and soul together make the person. The body is not a prison, and the soul is not a spark trapped by mistake.
catholic.image_of_god:
Every human being is made in the image of God, the imago Dei. For Catholics this grounds the dignity of the person from conception to natural death. The image is not first a set of abilities that the very young or the dying lack. It is the created relation to God that makes a human being capable of knowing and loving him.

Sin wounds the likeness, the holiness that should shine in the image, but it does not erase the image itself. Grace restores and raises it toward the likeness of Christ, who is the perfect Image of the Father. Catholic teaching on justice, the works of mercy, and the rights of the poor rests on this doctrine as much as teaching on worship does.
catholic.free_will:
Catholics teach that human beings have free will. Grace does not cancel it. After the Fall the will is weakened and inclined to sin, yet it remains a true will. A person can accept or refuse the grace offered. Cooperation with grace is itself a gift, not a private achievement beside God.

This is why the Church speaks of both God's initiative and human responsibility, of mortal sin as a free turning away, and of merit as God crowning his own gifts. Predestination is not read as a script that makes prayer and choice theatrical. The moral life, confession, and the call to conversion all assume a freedom that is real and that needs healing.
catholic.mortal_and_venial_sin:
Catholics distinguish mortal sin from venial sin. Mortal sin is a grave matter, done with full knowledge and deliberate consent, that destroys the life of sanctifying grace in the soul. Venial sin wounds that life without destroying it. The distinction is pastoral as well as doctrinal: it tells a person when Reconciliation is required before receiving Communion and when daily conversion still needs work.

No one is asked to treat every fault as equal. Habit, fear, and ignorance can lessen blame. At the same time, Catholics are warned against treating grave matter as light. Charity is the life of the soul. What kills charity is mortal. What leaves charity wounded but alive is venial. The sacrament of Reconciliation is the ordinary remedy for mortal sin after Baptism.
catholic.total_depravity:
Catholics do not use total depravity as their own name for the Fall. They speak of a wounded nature and of concupiscence. Human beings cannot save themselves or reach the vision of God by natural powers. They can still know some moral truth, keep some outward justice, and recognize God's existence, even while that knowledge is darkened and that will is bent.

The Council of Trent rejected the claim that free will was extinguished or that every act of the sinner is itself a sin. Catholic preaching therefore calls for conversion without saying that the image of God has been annihilated. Grace is necessary from first to last. It finds something to heal, not a ruin in which nothing human remains.
catholic.scripture:
Sacred Scripture is the written Word of God, inspired by the Holy Spirit and entrusted to the Church. Catholics read the Old and New Testaments as one story fulfilled in Christ. The Bible is not a free-standing authority over against the Church that received it, nor a mere record of religious experience. God is its author, and so are the human writers he employed.

Liturgy is soaked in Scripture: readings, psalms, prayers, and the words of the Mass itself. Private reading is encouraged. Interpretation is guided by the living tradition and the Magisterium so that the same faith is handed on. Catholics do not treat every verse as a separate law isolated from the whole canon and from the creed.
catholic.canon:
The canon of Scripture, for Catholics, includes the books of the Old Testament received from the Church's ancient Latin and Greek Bibles, together with the New Testament. That Old Testament includes the deuterocanonical books. The canon is closed. The Church does not add later writings as a new Bible, even when she honors them as spiritual reading.

Councils and popes confirmed this list. Catholics know that other communities use a shorter Old Testament. They still read those extra books as Scripture in the Mass and in doctrine, not as optional appendix. The canon is an act of the Church recognizing the books God gave, not a committee inventing a library.
catholic.sola_scriptura:
Catholics do not confess Scripture alone as the sole rule of faith. They confess Scripture and Tradition as two streams of the one Word of God, interpreted authentically by the Magisterium. Nothing in Tradition is held to contradict Scripture. Scripture remains the supreme written witness. It is read inside the Church that compiled it and preaches it.

This is why Catholics appeal to creeds, councils, liturgy, and the Fathers together with the Bible. Private reading is good. Private judgment that sets a reader over the Church's faith is not how Catholics think the canon itself came to be recognized. The three together, Scripture, Tradition, and the teaching office, are meant to serve one Gospel.
catholic.inspiration:
Catholics teach that the sacred books are inspired, God-breathed. The Holy Spirit so moved the human authors that what they wrote is what God wanted written, without turning them into pens without minds. Each book has a true human style and a true divine message.

Inspiration covers the books as the Church received them, in the sense intended by God and expressed by the writers. It is not a claim that every copyist's spelling is dictated, or that every ancient turn of phrase is a modern science text. The same Spirit who inspired the text lives in the Church that proclaims it.
catholic.inerrancy:
Catholics teach the inerrancy of Scripture in what God intended to teach for the sake of salvation. The Bible does not deceive. How that truth is expressed follows the genres and the ways of speaking of the human authors. The Church has insisted both that Scripture is true and that it must be read as the literature it is, not as a manual of every secular science.

Catholic interpreters differ on how far inerrancy extends into historical and cosmological detail. Official language holds that the books teach truth without error for the sake of our salvation. That is the claim Catholics are asked to receive, together with reverence for the text as God's Word rather than as a quarry of isolated proofs.
catholic.apocrypha:
What many call the Apocrypha Catholics call the deuterocanonical books: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, First and Second Maccabees, and portions of Esther and Daniel. They are read as Scripture in the Catholic canon, used in the lectionary, and cited in doctrine, including prayer for the dead and the praise of Wisdom.

Catholics know these books were disputed in antiquity and are omitted from many Protestant Bibles. They still receive them because the Church that recognized the New Testament also prayed these Old Testament books. They are not a second-class Bible. They are part of the one canon.
catholic.open_canon:
Catholics teach a closed canon. Public revelation that binds the whole Church is complete in Christ and in the apostolic witness fixed in Scripture and Tradition. Later saints, councils, and private revelations do not add books to the Bible or new articles that correct the apostles.

The Church can define more clearly what was already given. She cannot invent a new testament. Writings after the apostles may be holy and useful. They are not Scripture. This is why Catholics honor mystics and apparitions only after testing, and never as a rival canon.
catholic.continuing_revelation:
Catholics distinguish public revelation, finished with the apostles, from private revelation, which may help a person or an age but does not complete or correct the deposit of faith. Approved apparitions, such as those the Church has judged worthy of belief, do not stand beside the Gospel as a second source of dogma.

The Spirit still guides the Church into a deeper grasp of what was given once. That guidance is not new public revelation. Charisms continue. The canon does not grow. Catholics are free, within obedience, to take or leave a given private revelation. They are not free to treat the creed as unfinished business waiting for a later prophet.
catholic.hermeneutics:
Interpretation of Scripture, for Catholics, happens in the Church. The literal sense, what the human authors meant, is the foundation. Spiritual senses flow from it. The text is read in the unity of the whole canon, in the living tradition, and with attention to the analogy of faith, the coherence of doctrine.

The Magisterium does not replace study. It guards the faith those studies serve. Historical work is welcomed when it serves the text rather than emptying it. A Catholic reader is not forbidden to struggle with hard passages. He is asked not to set a private theory against the creed the Church has always preached from those same books.
catholic.tradition:
Sacred Tradition is the handing on of the Gospel in the Church's life: her liturgy, creeds, Fathers, and constant teaching, not a stack of extra secrets beside the Bible. Catholics hold that the apostles transmitted what they received from Christ in writing and in preaching, and that this living transmission continues under the Spirit.

Tradition is not whatever a later age finds convenient. It is measured by Scripture and by the Church's own earlier faith. When Catholics say Scripture and Tradition, they mean one deposit. Popular customs can grow and fade. The apostolic Tradition does not.
catholic.magisterium:
The Magisterium is the Church's teaching office, belonging to the bishops in communion with the Pope, and in a unique way to the Pope himself. Its task is to guard, expound, and apply the deposit of faith, not to invent a new one. Ordinary preaching, catechisms, and solemn definitions all belong to this office in different degrees of weight.

Catholics are asked to receive defined dogma as irreformable and to give religious assent to the ordinary teaching of pope and bishops on faith and morals. Disagreement among theologians exists. It does not dissolve the office. The Magisterium is service to the Word, not a third source above it.
catholic.papal_primacy:
Papal primacy is the Catholic confession that the Bishop of Rome, as successor of Peter, holds a real and lasting primacy of jurisdiction over the whole Church. It is more than a primacy of honor. The Pope is pastor of the universal Church, the visible principle of unity among the bishops and the faithful.

This ministry is understood as Christ's gift for communion, not as a human empire. Ecumenical councils and the daily life of dioceses remain real. Eastern Catholic churches keep their own rites under this same primacy. Catholics know other Christians reject the claim. They still hold that without Peter's successor the college of bishops lacks the head the Lord gave it.
catholic.papal_infallibility:
Papal infallibility is a narrowly defined charism. When the Pope speaks ex cathedra, that is, as supreme pastor, defining a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, he is preserved from error by the Spirit. The gift does not make every papal sermon, interview, or administrative act infallible.

The same infallibility belongs to the episcopal college with the Pope, especially in ecumenical council. Catholics are not asked to treat the Pope as a private oracle. They are asked to receive those rare solemn definitions as the Church's own faith. The dogma was defined in 1870; the practice it names is older than the definition.
catholic.ecumenical_councils:
Catholics recognize twenty-one ecumenical councils, from Nicaea to Vatican II, as solemn acts of the college of bishops with the Pope. Not every gathering of bishops is a council of this rank. Those that are bind the Church in the measure of their definitions and of the reception the Magisterium gives them.

Earlier councils on the Trinity and Christ remain the foundation. Later councils on grace, the sacraments, and the Church unfold the same faith. Vatican II is received as a true council. Catholics differ in how they apply it. They do not treat the first seven councils as the only ones that count.
catholic.apostolic_succession:
Apostolic succession is the unbroken handing on of the episcopal office from the apostles through the laying on of hands. Catholic bishops are held to stand in that line. Through them the Church remains apostolic not only in doctrine but in her visible ministry. Holy Orders depends on this succession.

Succession without the apostolic faith would be an empty shell, and Catholics also insist on continuity of teaching. The point of the doctrine is that the Church is not a later club reconstructing Jesus from texts. She is the same body, with shepherds whose office came from those Christ sent.
catholic.priesthood_authority:
Catholics speak of the sacred power given in Holy Orders. By ordination a man is configured to Christ the High Priest and is able to act in the person of Christ the Head in the sacraments that require that office, above all the Eucharist and Reconciliation. This power is a gift of the Spirit, not a personal talent or a community's delegation.

It exists for service. It does not make the priest a mediator who replaces Christ. It makes him an instrument through whom Christ continues his priesthood. The common priesthood of the faithful is real and different in kind from this ministerial priesthood. Both share in the one priesthood of Christ.
catholic.church:
Catholics call the Church the people of God, the Body of Christ, and the temple of the Spirit. She is a visible communion with a hidden depth, not a mere association of the like-minded. Christ founded her on the apostles, with Peter as their head, and she continues as a sacramental body in history.

The Church is holy because of Christ and the Spirit, while her members are sinners. She is the ordinary place of salvation and the mother who bears the faithful through Word and sacrament. To be Catholic is to belong to this communion, not only to hold a private list of doctrines.
catholic.one_true_church:
Catholics teach that the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, governed by the successor of Peter and by the bishops in communion with him. This is the Catholic way of saying that the Church Christ founded continues fully in this communion, with all the gifts he willed for her.

The same teaching recognizes that many elements of sanctification and truth exist outside her visible bounds. Other Christians are not treated as empty of grace. The claim is not that every Catholic is holier than every other Christian. It is that the fullness of the means of salvation is found in the Catholic Church.
catholic.great_apostasy:
Catholics reject the idea that the Church as a whole fell into a great apostasy and had to be refounded from nothing. They confess the indefectibility of the Church: she can be wounded by sin and error in her members, even in high office, but she cannot cease to be Christ's Church or lose the Gospel and the sacraments.

Reform is a constant need. Schism and heresy are real histories. None of that is read as the death of the Church between the apostles and a later restorer. The gates of hell shall not prevail is taken as a promise about this visible, sacramental body, not only about an invisible fellowship.
catholic.marks_of_the_church:
Catholics confess four marks of the Church in the Creed: one, holy, catholic, and apostolic. She is one in faith, sacraments, and visible government. She is holy in her source and in the saints, though her members sin. She is catholic, universal in mission and in the fullness of the faith. She is apostolic in origin, teaching, and succession.

These marks are not slogans. They are tests and gifts. Unity is visible, not only inward. Catholicity is more than geography. Apostolicity is more than reading the New Testament. The marks describe the Church Catholics believe they belong to, and they judge reform by fidelity to them.
catholic.visible_and_invisible_church:
Catholics insist that the Church is a visible communion, with creed, sacraments, and shepherds, not only an invisible set of the truly elect. The invisible life of grace is real, and God is not bound to the visible signs. Still, Christ founded a people one can point to in history.

The distinction between the Church as she appears and the saints known to God alone is admitted. It is not used to dissolve the visible body into a purely spiritual club. Membership in the visible Church and life in sanctifying grace are meant to go together. When they do not, the tragedy is named rather than made into a second, hidden church that replaces the first.
catholic.polity:
Catholic church government is episcopal and hierarchical. Each diocese has a bishop as its chief shepherd. The bishops together, with and under the Pope, care for the whole Church. Parishes, religious orders, and lay movements live inside this structure rather than beside it as equals in jurisdiction.

Hierarchy here means sacred order for communion, not a claim that clergy are better Christians. Synods and councils are part of this polity. So is the ordinary authority of the diocesan bishop. Catholics can argue about how collegiality and primacy should be exercised. They do not treat the Church as a federation of independent congregations.
catholic.local_church:
The local church in Catholic speech is first the diocese gathered around the bishop, with the Eucharist as its center. The parish is the usual place most of the faithful live that life: Sunday Mass, baptisms, catechesis, and the burial of the dead.

A parish is not an independent church. It belongs to the bishop and, through him, to the whole Catholic communion. Personal parishes, religious houses, and movements add other local shapes. The principle remains: the Church is realized in a place without being reduced to that place.
catholic.church_discipline:
Church discipline in Catholic life includes the sacrament of Reconciliation, canonical penalties, and, in grave cases, excommunication. Excommunication is a medicinal penalty that bars a person from the sacraments until reconciliation. It does not claim to settle the person's eternal fate.

Bishops and the Holy See apply the law of the Church for the sake of the common good and the good of the sinner. Discipline can be mild or severe, wisely or poorly used. Catholics do not treat the Church as unable to bind and loose in this world. They also teach that penalties aim at conversion, not at theater.
catholic.ecumenism:
Catholics are committed to ecumenism as a response to Christ's prayer for unity. Other baptized Christians are called separated brethren, brothers and sisters who share real gifts of grace and truth while remaining outside full communion. Dialogue, prayer together where it is allowed, and cooperation in works of mercy are official Catholic policy.

Ecumenism is not indifferentism. The Catholic Church does not regard all communions as equal embodiments of the one Church. She seeks a unity that includes shared faith, sacraments, and apostolic ministry. How that will look remains a matter of hope and work, not of pretending the divisions are already gone.
catholic.schism:
Schism is the refusal of submission to the Roman Pontiff or of communion with the members of the Church subject to him. Catholics distinguish it from heresy, which is the obstinate denial of a revealed truth, and from apostasy, which is the total repudiation of the faith. A person or community may fall into one without the others, though they often travel together.

Healing schism is a duty of charity and of truth. The Church names some breaks with sorrow and continues to recognize baptism and, in some cases, other sacraments beyond her visible bounds. Schism is treated as a wound in the Body, not as a neutral preference among brands.
catholic.ordination:
Ordination is the sacrament of Holy Orders, by which the mission Christ entrusted to the apostles continues in the Church. Through the laying on of hands and the prayer of the bishop, a man is configured to Christ and given a sacred office as bishop, priest, or deacon. Catholics do not treat this as a community's hire of a speaker. It is a sacrament that changes the man with an indelible character.

Only a bishop can ordain. The Church holds that she has no authority to confer priestly or episcopal ordination on women. Ordination is for service of Word and sacrament, not for personal rank. A validly ordained man remains ordained even if he is later forbidden to exercise the office.
catholic.priesthood:
Catholics distinguish the common priesthood of all the baptized from the ministerial priesthood of those in Holy Orders. Both share in the one priesthood of Christ. The ministerial priest acts in the person of Christ the Head when he consecrates the Eucharist and when he absolves sins. He is not a substitute for Christ and not a mere chairman of the assembly.

The ministerial priesthood exists to gather, teach, sanctify, and shepherd the priestly people. It does not cancel the dignity of the laity. Parishes live by both: the priest at the altar and in confession, the faithful offering their lives with that same sacrifice.
catholic.episcopacy:
A bishop is a successor of the apostles and the ordinary shepherd of a diocese. By episcopal ordination he receives the fullness of the sacrament of Orders. With the other bishops and the Pope he cares for the whole Church. He is the chief preacher, the minister of Confirmation and Orders, and the visible center of unity in his local church.

Catholic episcopacy is not a late management tier. It is how the apostolic office continues. Auxiliary bishops and retired bishops share the order without always holding a diocese of their own. The bishop's authority is pastoral and sacramental before it is administrative.
catholic.deacons:
A deacon is ordained for service of the Word, the liturgy, and charity, not to the priesthood. He may preach, baptize, witness marriages, and bury the dead. He does not consecrate the Eucharist or absolve sins. The Church now has both transitional deacons, on the way to priesthood, and permanent deacons, often married men.

The permanent diaconate was restored in the Latin Church after Vatican II. Deacons are clergy, not lay volunteers in a stole. Their ministry is meant to keep the Church's face turned toward the poor and toward the proclamation of the Gospel in daily life.
catholic.papacy:
The Pope is the Bishop of Rome, successor of Peter, and pastor of the universal Church. Catholics call him the Supreme Pontiff and the Holy Father. His office is to confirm the brethren and to be the visible principle of unity among the bishops and the faithful. He is not a fourth person of the Trinity and not the source of the other bishops' orders.

The Pope governs with ordinary and immediate authority, ordinarily through the Roman Curia and in communion with the episcopal college. Infallibility attaches only to rare solemn definitions of faith and morals. Daily papal teaching asks religious assent without being, in every sentence, a dogma.
catholic.priesthood_of_believers:
The common priesthood of the faithful is the share in Christ's priesthood given to every baptized person. Catholics offer their work, suffering, and prayer with the offering of the Mass. They are a priestly people, called to holiness and to witness, without being ordained ministers.

This common priesthood and the ministerial priesthood differ in essence and not only in degree. One does not replace the other. Lay apostolates, parents as first teachers of the faith, and the offering of Sunday worship all belong to this priestly dignity of the baptized.
catholic.clerical_celibacy:
In the Latin Church, priests are ordinarily chosen from men who have freely embraced celibacy for the sake of the kingdom. The discipline is ancient in the West and is held as a gift that frees a priest for undivided service. It is a law of the Latin Church, not a dogma that could never be otherwise.

Eastern Catholic churches ordain married men to the priesthood while reserving the episcopacy to celibates. The Latin Church also admits some married priests, chiefly former Anglican or Protestant clergy received into Catholic communion. Bishops in every Catholic rite are chosen from the celibate. Celibacy is not contempt for marriage. Marriage remains a sacrament.
catholic.baptism:
Baptism is the first sacrament of initiation. By water and the Spirit it remits original sin and all personal sin, gives sanctifying grace, incorporates a person into Christ and the Church, and leaves an indelible character. Catholics confess one Baptism. It is not repeated.

The ordinary minister is a priest or deacon, but in necessity anyone may baptize with the right intention and the Trinitarian form. Baptism is necessary for salvation in the sense the Church has always taught, while God is not bound by his own sacraments. Catechumens, those who die for the faith without water, and those who sincerely seek God are entrusted to his mercy under related headings of desire and blood.
catholic.infant_baptism:
Infant baptism is the Church's ordinary practice for the children of Catholic families. The child is given grace before personal faith can be articulated, and the parents and godparents promise to raise the child in that faith. Catholics see this as the New Covenant counterpart to belonging to the people of God from the start of life.

The practice assumes later catechesis, Confirmation, and a personal appropriation of the gift. An unbaptized adult is not baptized without personal faith and conversion. Infant baptism is not a charm. It is the beginning of a life that must be lived.
catholic.mode_of_baptism:
Catholics baptize by immersion, pouring, or sprinkling, using water and the words 'I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.' Pouring on the forehead is the most common Latin practice. Immersion is fully valid and is used in some places and rites.

The amount of water is not the essence. The water, the Trinitarian form, and the intention to do what the Church does are the essence. Eastern Catholic rites more often immerse. The Latin Church does not treat pouring as a lesser Baptism.
catholic.confirmation:
Confirmation completes Baptism by a special gift of the Holy Spirit for witness and maturity in the Christian life. In the Latin Church the bishop is the ordinary minister, and the sacrament is often given to adolescents, though it may be given earlier. The matter is anointing with chrism and the laying on of hands.

Eastern Catholics usually confer Confirmation, which they call Chrismation, together with infant Baptism. The doctrine is the same: the Spirit seals the baptized. Confirmation is not a Catholic graduation ceremony. It is a sacrament that marks the person for mission.
catholic.confession:
The sacrament of Reconciliation, also called Confession or Penance, is the ordinary way baptized Catholics are restored to grace after mortal sin. The penitent confesses grave sins by kind and number, as far as memory allows, to a priest, who gives absolution in Christ's name and assigns a penance.

Venial sins may be forgiven in many ways, including the penitential rite of Mass, yet confession of them is encouraged. Perfect contrition restores grace before the sacrament when it includes the intention to confess. The seal of confession binds the priest absolutely. Catholics are obliged to confess mortal sins at least once a year and before receiving Communion.
catholic.anointing_of_the_sick:
Anointing of the Sick is the sacrament by which the Church commends the seriously ill to the suffering and risen Christ. A priest anoints the forehead and hands with the oil of the sick and prays for healing of soul and, if it be God's will, of body. It is not reserved for the last moments of life, though it includes what was once commonly called Extreme Unction.

Those in danger from illness or old age may receive it, and it may be repeated. When joined to Confession and Viaticum it prepares a person for death. The sacrament is a prayer of the Church, not a guarantee of physical cure and not a replacement for medical care.
catholic.holy_orders:
Holy Orders is the sacrament that confers the ministries of bishop, priest, and deacon. It is one sacrament in three degrees. The bishop has the fullness of the order. The priest is his coworker in the sacerdotal office. The deacon is ordained for service. The character given is permanent.

Catholics hold that only a baptized man may be validly ordained to this sacrament as the Church has received it. The sacrament is not a right claimed from the community. It is a gift Christ gives through the Church for the sake of the Eucharist and the flock.
catholic.matrimony:
Matrimony is the sacrament in which a baptized man and a baptized woman give themselves to one another in a covenant ordered to the good of the spouses and to the procreation and education of children. The ministers of the sacrament are the couple themselves. The priest or deacon assists and blesses in the Latin Church.

The bond is indissoluble when the marriage is valid and consummated. Annulment is a judgment that no sacramental bond arose, not a Catholic divorce. Mixed marriages are possible under conditions. Matrimony is a vocation and a path of holiness, not a private contract the Church merely registers.
catholic.sacraments:
Catholics confess seven sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Reconciliation, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony. They are efficacious signs of grace instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church. They give the grace they signify when received with the right disposition.

The Eucharist holds the center. The others either lead to it, restore the life it feeds, or order the Church's mission and the family. Sacramentals, such as blessings and holy water, prepare for the sacraments and do not replace them. Seven is not a random number. It is the Church's count of the rites that bear this weight.
catholic.real_presence:
Catholics confess the Real Presence: after the consecration the bread and wine are the Body and Blood of Christ. The change is called transubstantiation. What appears remains the appearances of bread and wine. What is present is Christ, whole and entire, in each kind.

This presence remains as long as the appearances remain. Hence reservation in the tabernacle, Eucharistic adoration, and careful reverence for fragments and for the Precious Blood. The Real Presence is not a metaphor for a community's memory and not a physical tearing of Christ's glorified body. It is the sacramental presence of the same Lord who rose from the dead.
catholic.eucharistic_sacrifice:
The Mass is the sacrifice of the Eucharist, the making present of Christ's one sacrifice of the Cross. It does not repeat Calvary as if the first offering were incomplete. The same Priest and the same Victim are present under the signs of the Church's offering. The Mass is also a sacred banquet.

Catholics speak of the sacrifice of the Mass as propitiatory for the living and the dead, always in dependence on the Cross. The priest offers in the person of Christ. The faithful offer with him. Sunday after Sunday the Church lives from this one act made present, not from a new redemption invented each morning.
catholic.closed_communion:
Catholics practice closed communion in the sense that ordinary reception of the Eucharist is for those in full communion with the Catholic Church who are baptized, believe what the Church believes of the sacrament, and are in a state of grace. The Eucharist is a sign of unity already given, not a means of creating that unity while faith and governance remain divided.

Limited exceptions exist, under strict conditions, for some Eastern Christians and, in danger of death or other grave need, for certain other baptized persons who request the sacrament and hold the Catholic faith concerning it. Hospitality at the table is real. It is not the same as an open invitation that ignores communion.
catholic.foot_washing:
The mandatum is the Holy Thursday washing of feet, recalling Christ's act at the Last Supper. It is a solemn sign of service inside the Mass of the Lord's Supper, not an eighth sacrament. Bishops and pastors wash feet as a public imitation of the Lord who came to serve.

Catholic practice has varied in who is chosen to have their feet washed. The rite teaches humility and charity. It does not replace the Eucharist it accompanies. Most Catholics encounter it once a year, if at all, and they are not bound to it as they are bound to the Sunday Mass.
catholic.temples:
Catholics do not call their ordinary places of worship temples in the sense of a restored Jerusalem sanctuary or of buildings reserved for hidden rites. The church building is a house for the Eucharist and for the assembly. The body of the Christian is also called a temple of the Holy Spirit.

Christ himself is the new Temple. The Mass is the sacrifice of the new covenant. Catholic architecture, tabernacle, and altar exist so that this presence can be adored and this sacrifice offered. Pilgrimage shrines and great basilicas are still churches, not a second system beside the parish Mass.
catholic.liturgy:
Liturgy is the public worship of the Church, above all the Mass, the sacraments, and the Liturgy of the Hours. In the Latin Church the ordinary form is the Mass of the Roman Rite. Eastern Catholic churches celebrate their own rites with equal dignity. Liturgy is not a parish performance. It is the action of Christ the Head and of his Body.

The Church regulates the rites so that the same faith is prayed everywhere. Legitimate variety of language, music, and custom lives inside that order. Private devotion is encouraged. It does not replace the liturgy, which Catholics call the source and summit of the Church's life.
catholic.prayer:
Prayer is the raising of the heart and mind to God. Catholics pray in the liturgy and in private: adoration, thanksgiving, petition, and contrition. The Our Father is the pattern Christ gave. The prayer of the Church includes the Hours, the Rosary, novenas, and silent recollection before the tabernacle.

Prayer is addressed to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. It also includes asking the saints to intercede. Vocal prayer, meditation, and contemplative prayer are all honored. Prayer is not magic and not a substitute for justice. It is the life of charity speaking to God.
catholic.liturgical_calendar:
The liturgical year is the Church's way of living the mystery of Christ across time: Advent, Christmas, Lent, the Easter Triduum, Easter, and Ordinary Time, together with feasts of the Lord, of Mary, and of the saints. Sundays are the first feast. The calendar is not decoration. It is catechesis in time.

Fasts, solemnities, and memorials teach the same Gospel the lectionary reads. Local calendars add patrons and dedications. Catholics are not bound to treat every optional memorial as equal to Easter. They are bound to keep Sunday and the holy days of obligation of their region.
catholic.sabbath:
Catholics fulfill the meaning of the Sabbath by keeping Sunday, the Lord's Day, the day of the Resurrection. The third commandment is lived as rest from unnecessary work and as participation in the Eucharist. Sunday is not a mere substitute Saturday. It is the first day, the beginning of the new creation.

The Church does not require Saturday rest as the old covenant Sabbath. She does require that Sunday be kept holy. Where civil work makes Sunday Mass impossible, the pastor may judge another time. The principle remains: the risen Lord's day gathers the Church.
catholic.sunday_worship:
Sunday obligation is the duty of Catholics to take part in Mass on Sunday and on holy days of obligation, unless excused by a serious reason. The obligation is to the Mass, not to a vague hour of religious feeling. Those who cannot attend are asked to keep the day holy as they can.

The obligation names how serious the Eucharist is for Catholic life. It is not meant as a tax. Missing Mass through indifference is treated as grave matter. Care for the sick, the imprisoned, and those without a priest is part of the same Sunday faith.
catholic.icons:
Catholics honor sacred images: icons, statues, paintings of Christ, Mary, and the saints. The honor given to the image passes to the one depicted. It is not the worship given to God alone. The second commandment is not read as a ban on all religious art. It is read as a ban on idolatry.

Eastern Catholics keep a strong iconographic tradition. The Latin Church uses statues more freely. Iconoclasm is rejected. So is treating an object as a charm. Images teach the Incarnation: the unseen God has made himself visible in Christ, and matter can bear his memory.
catholic.veneration:
Veneration is the honor Catholics give to the saints and to holy things. Worship, adoration, belongs to God alone. Classic language calls worship of God latria, honor of the saints dulia, and the special honor of Mary hyperdulia. The words are scholastic. The distinction is lived in every Hail Mary that ends by asking her prayer, not her omnipotence.

Veneration includes images, relics, and feast days. It is meant to lead to imitation and to God. When it slides toward superstition, the Church corrects it. When it is refused as if the saints were rivals to Christ, Catholics answer that the friends of Christ are honored for his sake.
catholic.fasting:
Fasting and abstinence are penitential practices of the Church. In the Latin Church, Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fast and abstinence from meat for those bound by age and health. Fridays in Lent are days of abstinence, and other Fridays call for some penance. The details are set by conference of bishops and may vary.

Fasting is not a bargain with God. It trains the will, joins the Christian to the hungry, and accompanies prayer. Eastern Catholic fasting rules are often stricter and follow their own calendars. Dispensations exist because the point is conversion, not the breaking of the weak.
catholic.sacred_music:
Sacred music serves the liturgy. Gregorian chant has pride of place in the Roman Rite. Polyphony, hymnody, and other worthy forms are welcomed when they support the text and the action of the Mass rather than replace them with a concert. The assembly's singing is part of the rite.

Taste differs among Catholics, sometimes sharply. Official teaching asks for beauty, holiness, and universality, not for one decade's style as a new law. Music is for prayer. When it becomes entertainment or a badge of a party in the Church, it has left its office.
catholic.preaching:
The homily is the preaching proper to the Mass, ordinarily given by a bishop, priest, or deacon. It breaks open the readings and the mystery being celebrated so that the faithful can offer their lives with the sacrifice. Catholic preaching is bound to Scripture and to the Church's faith, not to the preacher's private platform.

Catechesis, missions, and spiritual conferences extend preaching beyond the Mass. The Church still treats the Sunday homily as a chief place where most Catholics hear the Word explained. A poor homily does not undo the Mass. It is still a failure of a real duty.
catholic.sign_of_the_cross:
The sign of the cross traces the cross on the body while naming the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. It is the Catholic's shortest creed and a blessing used at the start and end of prayer, at the Gospel, with holy water, and in trial. It confesses both the Trinity and the Crucified.

Latin Catholics touch forehead, breast, and shoulders. Eastern Catholics often use two or three fingers and move from right to left. The gesture is small. The faith it carries is not. Careless waving is not what the Church means by the sign.
catholic.rosary:
The Rosary is a meditative prayer in which Catholics recite decades of Hail Marys, with the Our Father and the Glory Be, while dwelling on the mysteries of Christ's life, death, and resurrection, and on Mary's share in them. It is a popular devotion, not a sacrament and not a substitute for the Mass.

Popes have commended it. Many saints have lived by it. Other Catholics pray little of it and remain fully Catholic. The Rosary is Christ-centered in intent: the mysteries are his, and the petitions ask Mary's intercession, not an independent power.
catholic.jesus_prayer:
The Jesus Prayer, 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner,' is at home in Eastern Catholic and Orthodox practice and is used by many Latin Catholics as well. It is a short, repeated prayer meant to descend from the lips to the heart. It is not required of anyone.

Catholics who adopt it treat it as a way of keeping the holy name and of asking mercy without many words. It sits beside, not above, the liturgy and the sacramental life. Spiritual fathers warn against treating any technique as a machine for visions.
catholic.mary:
Catholics honor the Blessed Virgin Mary as the Mother of God and the first among the saints. She is not a fourth person of the Trinity and not a rival redeemer. Her whole dignity comes from Christ. The Church calls her Mother of the Church and asks her prayers because she is the one who said yes at the Annunciation and stood at the Cross.

Catholic life is marked by her feasts, the Hail Mary, the Rosary, and countless titles such as Our Lady. Devotion varies in warmth from person to person. Doctrine does not. What the Church believes about Mary is a way of stating what she believes about her Son and about the Church.
catholic.theotokos:
Catholics confess Mary as Mother of God, Theotokos, because the one born of her is the eternal Son, one person who is true God and true man. The title was defended at Ephesus to protect the unity of Christ, not to make Mary the origin of the divine nature.

To refuse her this name, in Catholic hearing, is to divide the Lord into a man merely associated with God. Prayers that call her Mother of God are Christological before they are Marian. The child in her arms is the Word made flesh.
catholic.immaculate_conception:
The Immaculate Conception is the dogma that Mary, by a unique grace and by the merits of Christ, was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception. It is not the virgin birth of Jesus, with which it is often confused. It names her beginning, not his.

Catholics see this preservation as the fitting start of the woman who would give her flesh to the Savior. She is redeemed more perfectly, not excused from needing Christ. The feast on 8 December and the definition of 1854 fix a faith already long prayed in the Church.
catholic.assumption:
The Assumption is the dogma that Mary, at the end of her earthly life, was taken body and soul into heavenly glory. Whether she died first is not defined. The Church leans toward a death followed by this taking up, which Eastern Catholics know as the Dormition.

The Assumption is Mary's share in her Son's resurrection, given in advance of the general resurrection. It is not a claim that she raised herself. The feast on 15 August is a holy day in many countries. Catholic hope for the body is preached in her.
catholic.perpetual_virginity:
Catholics confess the perpetual virginity of Mary: virgin before, during, and after the birth of Jesus. The 'brothers' of the Lord in the Gospels are read as kin, not as sons of Mary. The doctrine is ancient in the creeds of the Church's prayer, not a late sentiment.

It does not deny the goodness of marriage. It marks this one vocation as wholly given to the Incarnation. Protestants often dispute the reading of those kinship texts. Catholics hold the reading that the liturgy and the Fathers handed on.
catholic.intercession_of_saints:
Catholics ask the intercession of the saints, as they ask living friends to pray, because the dead in Christ are alive in him. Prayer to a saint is a request for that person's prayer, not the adoration due to God. The saints hear by God's gift, not by a nature of their own that rivals his.

The practice belongs to the communion of saints. Christ remains the one Mediator. Those who belong to him can still plead for one another. Abuse and superstition are real temptations. They do not cancel the doctrine.
catholic.relics:
Relics are the bodies of the saints, or objects closely tied to them or to Christ. Catholics honor them because God has worked through the flesh of his friends and because the resurrection will raise that same flesh. Honor given to a relic is honor given to the person, and through the person to God.

The Church forbids selling relics as merchandise and warns against fraud. Relics are placed in altars by custom and carried in procession. They are not charms. They are memory in matter, consistent with a faith that is incarnational.
catholic.prayers_for_the_dead:
Catholics pray for the dead who die in God's friendship but still need purification. Masses, indulgences, almsgiving, and the suffrages of the Church are offered for them. The practice assumes both the communion of saints and a state after death that is not yet the fullness of heaven for everyone who is saved.

Prayer for the dead is not an attempt to overturn a damned will. It is charity across the border of death. Funerals, All Souls' Day, and the Memento of the Dead at Mass keep the duty public.
catholic.canonization_of_saints:
Canonization is the Church's solemn declaration that a person is with God and may be honored in the universal liturgy. It follows investigation of life, writings, and, in the ordinary modern process, miracles attributed to that person's intercession. Beatification permits a more limited honor.

Canonization does not make a saint. It recognizes one. The calendar of saints is a school of holiness, not a hall of celebrities. Catholics are not obliged to have a private devotion to every name in the martyrology. They are obliged to believe that God does raise up witnesses.
catholic.heaven:
Heaven is the state of those who see God face to face, the beatific vision, and live in perfect communion with the Trinity, the angels, and the saints. It is the fulfillment of charity, not a lounge of private rewards. The resurrection of the body belongs to this same hope, even though souls already enjoy God before that day.

Catholic teaching insists that heaven is gift, that it is personal and social, and that it cannot be imagined adequately. Images of feast, city, and rest are all true and all too small. The saints already share this life. The Church on earth walks toward it.
catholic.hell:
Hell is the state of definitive self-exclusion from God. Catholics teach that it is real, that it is eternal for those who die unrepentant in mortal sin, and that God predestines no one to it. The images of fire and outer darkness name a true ruin of the person who has refused Love to the end.

The Church prays for the salvation of all and does not publish a list of the damned. She also refuses to empty the warnings of Christ. Hell is not a temporary school. It is the possibility that freedom can say no forever.
catholic.purgatory:
Purgatory is the purification of those who die in God's grace but are not yet wholly ready for the vision of God. It is not a second chance for the unrepentant and not a third final destiny beside heaven and hell. It is the last healing of the saved.

The Church does not define the psychology or the timetable of this purification. She teaches that it exists, that it is painful and hopeful, and that the living can help the dead by prayer, especially the Mass. This is why Catholics speak of the poor souls and keep All Souls' Day.
catholic.intermediate_state:
Catholics teach a particular judgment at death. The soul meets Christ and is directed toward heaven, toward purification, or toward hell, while awaiting the resurrection of the body and the last judgment. This is the intermediate state in Catholic speech, though the word itself is less common than particular judgment.

The dead are not unconscious. The saints already see God. The souls in purification are alive in Christ and helped by the Church. The damned are excluded. All still await the raising of the flesh.
catholic.soul_sleep:
Catholics do not teach soul sleep. The dead in Christ are awake to God. The liturgy addresses the saints as living persons. Prayers for the dead assume that those souls can be helped now. Immortality here is gift and destiny, not a natural spark that never needed God.

Sleep is a Christian metaphor for death of the body. It is not, in Catholic doctrine, unconsciousness of the person between death and resurrection. The resurrection remains essential. It completes what the soul already knows or already lacks.
catholic.resurrection_of_the_dead:
Catholics confess the resurrection of the body. The same person who lived and died will live again, body and soul, in a glorified or a condemned flesh. Christ's resurrection is the pattern and the cause. This hope is why the Church treats the corpse with reverence and why she rejects both scorn for the body and fantasies of reincarnation.

The general resurrection is tied to the last day. Until then the dead exist as souls awaiting that completion, except for those already raised in a unique way, as the Church confesses of Christ and of Mary.
catholic.last_judgment:
The Last Judgment is the public disclosure of God's justice and mercy at the return of Christ, when the risen are judged and the kingdom is handed over in its fullness. It does not cancel the particular judgment. It reveals what was hidden and gathers the whole of history into one verdict.

Catholics preach this judgment as hope for the poor and as warning for the hard of heart. The works of mercy in Matthew 25 stand at the center of that preaching. Christ is the Judge because he is the Savior who was judged.
catholic.second_coming:
Catholics confess the Second Coming, the Parousia: Christ will return in glory to judge the living and the dead. The Church lives between Ascension and return. She does not date the day. She watches, celebrates the Eucharist, and prays Come, Lord Jesus.

Speculation that turns the Gospel into a timetable is discouraged. Denial that he will come is excluded. Every Mass already tastes the coming kingdom. The creed keeps the promise public.
catholic.millennium:
Catholics do not teach a coming earthly thousand-year reign of Christ in the sense of millenarianism condemned by the Church. The thousand years of Revelation is read, in the ordinary Catholic tradition, as the time of the Church or as a symbol of completeness, not as a future political age that postpones the last advent.

Christ already reigns. His kingdom is present in mystery and will be manifest at his return. Catholic hope is the new creation and the resurrection, not an intermediate Christian empire as the main object of faith.
catholic.rapture:
Catholics do not teach a secret rapture that removes believers from the world before a later public coming. They confess one return of Christ, the raising of the dead, and the gathering of the elect. Being caught up to meet the Lord is read as part of that one advent, not as a separate escape hatch years earlier.

Popular rapture schemes are known to many Catholics through the surrounding culture. They are not the Church's doctrine. Watchfulness remains. It is the watchfulness of servants at Mass and in charity, not of calendar watchers.
catholic.annihilation:
Catholics teach the eternal punishment of those who die in unrepented mortal sin, not the annihilation of the lost. The person is not erased. The exclusion from God is decisive and without a promised end. How to speak of that ruin without crude pictures is a pastoral task. The teaching itself stands.

Some Catholic theologians have hoped that hell might in fact be empty. The Church allows prayer for all. She has not replaced eternal punishment with extinction as doctrine. The gravity of freedom is the point.
catholic.new_creation:
Catholics hope for new heavens and a new earth, the fulfillment of creation rather than the discarding of it. The risen body and a transfigured world belong together. God will be all in all. This is not an escape from matter. It is matter redeemed.

Care for the poor and for the earth is framed by this hope without being reduced to politics. The Eucharist is already a sign of the new creation in bread and wine. The last pages of Scripture are read as promise, not as a comic-book ending.
catholic.marriage:
Marriage, for baptized spouses, is a sacrament: a covenant of life and love ordered to the good of the spouses and to children. It is exclusive, faithful, and open to life. The family is called a domestic church. Marriage is a vocation, not a private lifestyle contract.

The Church blesses many marriages and refuses some. Impediments, form, and consent matter because the bond is real. Preparation and support are pastoral duties. The ideal does not deny the wounds of actual households. It names what the sacrament is for.
catholic.divorce:
Catholics teach that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power. Civil divorce may be tolerated for civil effects and for safety. It does not free a person to marry again in the Church while the bond remains. Those living in a new union outside the Church are not free to receive Communion as a rule, though pastoral care continues.

An annulment is a finding that no sacramental marriage existed. It is not a Catholic word for divorce. The Orthodox practice of economia is not the Latin Church's law. The hardness of this teaching is felt. Catholics still hold the indissolubility Christ taught.
catholic.contraception:
The Catholic Church teaches that every act of marital intercourse should remain open to life, and that artificial contraception is wrong. Periodic abstinence for serious reasons, often called natural family planning, is permitted. The teaching rests on the meaning of the act as both unitive and procreative.

Many Catholics struggle with this doctrine or do not live it. Official teaching has not withdrawn it. Sterilization sought as a contraceptive means falls under the same judgment. Medicine that treats disease and only incidentally affects fertility is assessed differently. The norm is the full meaning of the conjugal act.
catholic.abortion:
Catholics teach that procured abortion is a grave moral evil because it takes an innocent human life. The unborn child is a person with the dignity of the image of God. The Church's canonical penalties, including latae sententiae excommunication in the Latin code for those who procure abortion when the conditions are met, mark the gravity.

Mercy for those who have been involved is also official teaching. Confession and return are held out without softening the judgment on the act. Political application varies among Catholics. The moral claim does not.
catholic.sexual_ethics:
Catholic sexual ethics is summed up as chastity: the successful integration of sexuality within the person, according to one's state of life. For the unmarried, that means abstinence from genital sexual acts. For the married, it means fidelity, honor of the spouse, and openness to life. The body is not a tool. It is the person made visible.

The Church holds that sexual acts belong in marriage between a man and a woman. Other uses of sex are judged contrary to that meaning. This teaching is widely contested even among Catholics. It remains the teaching they are asked to receive, together with compassion for those who find it costly.
catholic.tithing:
Catholics are bound to support the Church, but they are not bound by a universal law of a tenth as Israel was. Stewardship and offerings, Sunday collections, and care for the poor are the ordinary language. Some Catholics adopt a tithe as a personal discipline.

Simony is forbidden. The sacraments are not sold. Support is a duty of justice and gratitude. How much is a matter of circumstance and conscience, guided by the needs of the parish, the diocese, and the poor.
catholic.alcohol:
Catholics do not require abstinence from alcohol. Wine is used at the Eucharist. Temperance is the virtue: drink may be used with thanksgiving and must not master the person. Drunkenness is a sin. For some, complete abstinence is the only wise path, and that choice is honored.

Religious orders have known both cellar and fast. Cultures differ. Official teaching is measured use, not prohibition and not carelessness. The chalice at Mass is not a brief for excess at table.
catholic.pacifism:
The Catholic tradition's main frame for public force is the just war teaching: legitimate authority, just cause, right intention, last resort, proportionality, and care for noncombatants. At the same time the Church honors conscientious refusal to bear arms and praises peacemaking as blessed.

Recent popes have spoken with increasing severity about modern weapons and about war's human cost. Catholics differ on particular conflicts. They are not required to be pacifists. They are required not to treat war as a first tool or as exempt from moral law.
catholic.church_and_state:
